title: The Sea of Reeds
lead: Yam Suf, the sea Israel crossed when leaving Egypt (Exodus 14–15). Called the Red Sea in Greek and in most English Bibles, it is remembered across the Bible as the LORD's great act of rescue (Psalm 106:9; Isaiah 51:10; Hebrews 11:29).

sections.b: Yam Suf names more than one body of water. Israel crosses it leaving Egypt (Exodus 13–15), camps by it again after Elim (Numbers 33:10–11), and later travels "by the way of the Sea of Reeds" around Edom (Numbers 21:4). Solomon's fleet sails from Ezion-geber "on the shore of the Sea of Reeds" (1 Kings 9:26), which is the Gulf of Aqaba. The locusts of Egypt are blown into it (Exodus 10:19). The Greek translators called it the Red Sea, the name used in Acts 7:36 and Hebrews 11:29.
sections.refs: Exodus 10:19; Exodus 13:18; Exodus 15:4; Numbers 21:4; Numbers 33:10–11; 1 Kings 9:26; Acts 7:36; Hebrews 11:29

sections.b: The crossing becomes Israel's great memory of rescue. Joshua compares the Jordan crossing to it (Joshua 4:23), and Rahab says Canaan heard of it (Joshua 2:10). Psalms sing of the sea that looked and ran away (Psalm 114:3) and of God's path through the great waters (Psalm 77:19; 106:9–12; 136:13–15). Isaiah promises a new way through the sea (Isaiah 43:16–19; 51:10). Paul calls it a baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and Revelation's victors sing the song of Moses beside a sea of glass (Revelation 15:2–3).
